 ## Search results
Sampled softmax is compatible with NextItNet’s causal convolutional backbone: the original paper explicitly proposes it as an alternative to full-catalog softmax ([NextItNet](https://fajieyuan.github.io/papers/nextitnet6.pdf)). A 2024 analysis shows that sampled softmax already emphasizes high-scoring negatives through its gradients; temperature controls that emphasis, with excessively low temperatures allowing a few difficult negatives to dominate ([Wu et al., 2024](https://wujcan.github.io/papers/tois-ssm.pdf)). Thus, increasing negative count and tuning temperature provide a useful baseline before adding explicit mining. Scalable Cross-Entropy similarly targets informative catalog outputs using approximate maximum-inner-product search, although its efficiency and accuracy findings do not establish gains for this Electronics benchmark ([SCE, 2024](https://dspace.mit.edu/entities/publication/5392aca9-0bae-4176-9b3a-a8165957ba26)).

Hardness alone is unreliable evidence of negative relevance. UFNRec documents false negatives in sequential recommendation, but its teacher-based correction should not be imported into this single-model experiment ([UFNRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04116)). A 2026 contrastive-recommendation study uses a controlled hard/random mixture and filters both overly similar and overly distant candidates ([EMM](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0893608026004090)). Practical hypothesis, rather than an established NextItNet result: compare uniform sampled softmax against a modest mixture of random and moderately hard negatives scored by the same network; exclude padding, targets, and known training positives, and soften or discard extreme candidates rather than asserting they are true negatives. Keep inference unchanged and select by pinned macro validation HR@10 across all four categories. Lower training loss or larger positive–negative margins cannot establish ranking generalization.

---

NextItNet’s residual dilated convolutions capture short- and long-range dependencies without pooling, providing a natural backbone for adaptive context selection ([original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.05163)). Earlier research supplies direct precedents: [time-aware attentive memory networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.08598) use temporal gates for information filtering and state transitions; [user-adaptive layer selection](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/16518) explores personalized computation in deep sequential recommenders. These support investigating temporal gates and adaptive depth, but do not establish improvements on the specified Amazon benchmark.

Recent work reinforces the motivation. [MIMAR-SRec, AAAI 2026](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/38489) models intent across different contextual windows and addresses interaction, temporal and preference noise. [GDA-REIM, 2026](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0893608026001838) combines gated attention denoising with repetition–exploration intent modeling. [Frequency-Adaptive Dilated Convolution, CVPR 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.05369) demonstrates input-dependent dilation in vision; its relevance to recommendation is an architectural analogy, not recommendation evidence.

Research hypothesis: retain one jointly trained NextItNet per category and introduce causal, positionwise gates over convolutional features with different receptive fields. Condition gates on historical hidden states and observed timestamp gaps, allowing recent coherent activity to outweigh stale context while retaining useful longer dependencies. Repetition should mean recurring latent intent, since evaluation excludes seen-item candidates. Preserve padding masks and final-nonpadding readout. Compare temporal gating and receptive-field gating separately before combining them; select solely by macro validation HR@10 across all four categories. No retrieved study directly validates this exact adaptation.

---

Recent work supports incorporating item content into sequential recommendation, but the retrieved papers do not establish the exact combination of scratch-trained title/description encoding and a NextItNet backbone. [ConvRec (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04723) demonstrates attribute-aware convolutional sequence modeling with hierarchical neighborhood aggregation and linear computational/memory complexity; it motivates convolutional content integration, rather than a backbone replacement. [ITS-Rec (2025)](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/9/1748) combines titles, descriptions and reviews with sequential modeling, but uses BERT and a SASRec-derived architecture. Its strongest textual contribution comes from reviews, unavailable here, so its reported gains cannot be transferred directly.

Complementarity and substitution require particular caution. [MMSC (2025; revised 2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22268) explicitly treats co-view/co-purchase associations as noisy, sparse supervision; its foundation-model and LLM-assisted components fall outside this experiment’s constraints. [SCRM (2024 revision)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.14957) constructs relation graphs using distinct click and purchase behaviors, then denoises them. Neither establishes that title similarity or ordinary chronological adjacency alone identifies functional compatibility, substitution or user needs.

A constraint-compatible hypothesis, inferred from these findings: retain NextItNet’s causal dilated convolutions; jointly train a small randomly initialized token-embedding/pooling encoder over available titles and descriptions; fuse its projected output with item-ID embeddings inside one network. Use the resulting representations consistently for history encoding and candidate scoring, with one checkpoint per category.
